lmsArticle.title: System Design HLD Example: Collaborative Document Editing (Google Docs)
lmsArticle.subtitle: A senior-level HLD for real-time collaborative editing with Operational Transformation (OT) and conflict resolution.
lmsArticle.excerpt: Real-time collaborative editing relies on **Operational Transformation (OT)** or **CRDTs** to resolve concurrent edits without data loss. The core trade-off is **Latency vs. Consistency**: we use optimistic local updates for zero-latency typing and a centralized OT server to ensure all clients eventually converge to the exact same document state.
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

Real-time collaborative editing relies on **Operational Transformation (OT)** or **CRDTs** to resolve concurrent edits without data loss. The core trade-off is **Latency vs. Consistency**: we use optimistic local updates for zero-latency typing and a centralized OT server to ensure all clients eventually converge to the exact same document state.

Imagine two users, Alice and Bob, are editing the same sentence: "The…

This walkthrough focuses on **The "Hello World" Race Condition**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Imagine two users, Alice and Bob, are editing the same sentence: "The cat is happy." Alice wants to change it to "The fat cat is happy," so she inserts "fat " at position 4.
- Simultaneously, Bob wants to change it to "The cat is very happy," so he inserts "very " at position 11.
- Alice's Edit: Server applies INSERT("fat ", pos:4) .

**Concepts in play:** system-design-hld-architectures, caching, database-sharding, consistency-replication

## Stage 1 — Real-Time Collaboration: Use Cases & Requirements

- Actors - Author / Editor: Creates and modifies document content in real-time.
- - Collaborator: Views live changes and contributes simultaneously.
- - Viewer: Consumes the document without editing rights but still expects live updates.
- Functional Requirements - Real-Time Editing: Multiple users can edit the same document simultaneously.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Functional Requirements - Real-Time Editing: Multiple users can edit the same document simultaneously.

## Stage 2 — Basics: Operational Transformation (OT)

- Operational Transformation is the "classic" approach used by Google Docs.
- The core idea is that the server doesn't just apply an operation; it transforms it against all other operations that happened since the client's last known version.
- Every operation is represented as a triple: (Type, Position, Value) .
- When the server receives an operation based on version V , but the current server version is V+k , it runs the new operation through a transform function T(op new, op concurrent) for all $k$ operations.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** When the server receives an operation based on version V , but the current server version is V+k , it runs the new operation through a transform function T(op new, op concurrent) for all $k$ operations.

## Stage 3 — Mechanics: The Transform Matrix

- To implement OT, you must define how every operation type interacts with every other operation type.
- Insert: If User A inserts at position 5 and User B inserts at position 10, no change is needed for A, but B's position must be incremented by the length of A's insert.
- Delete: If a character is deleted before an insert, the insert position must be decremented.
- Delete: If both users delete the same character, the second operation becomes a "no-op" to avoid double-deletion.

*Applies **database-sharding** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Delete: If both users delete the same character, the second operation becomes a "no-op" to avoid double-deletion.

## Stage 4 — Estimations & Design Goals

- The Math of Real-Time Sync - Average Typist: 60 words per minute $\approx 5$ characters per second.
- - Active Users per Doc: 10 (average) to 1,000 (hot docs).
- - Traffic per Doc: 10 users 5 chars/sec = 50 operations/sec .
- - Fan-out: Every 1 operation must be broadcast to the other 9 users.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Fan-out: Every 1 operation must be broadcast to the other 9 users.

## Stage 5 — High-Level Design: The Centralized OT Architecture

- The following architecture utilizes a centralized "Orderer" to ensure all operations are sequenced correctly.
- The diagram above captures the full topology.
- The critical insight is the separation of concerns : WebSocket Servers handle raw TCP connections and serialization, the OT Service is the single stateful arbiter that runs all transformations, and Redis Pub/Sub is the…

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "High-Level Design: The Centralized OT Architecture - Subsystem Overview",
  "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persistent datastores.",
  "view": "high-level",
  "pattern": "microservices",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "edge", "label": "Edge Traffic Ingress", "tone": "slate" },
    { "id": "services", "label": "Stateless Microservices", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "data", "label": "Datastore Infrastructure", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "gw", "component": "api-gateway", "label": "API Gateway", "group": "edge", "badge": "TLS & Auth" },
    { "id": "app", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Domain Service", "group": "services", "badge": "Stateless" },
    { "id": "cache", "component": "redis", "label": "Redis Cache", "group": "data", "badge": "Sub-ms Reads" },
    { "id": "db", "component": "postgres", "label": "Transactional DB", "group": "data", "badge": "ACID Log" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "gw", "to": "app", "kind": "request", "label": "gRPC Request" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "cache", "kind": "read", "label": "Cache Lookups" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "db", "kind": "write", "label": "Durable Write" }
  ],
  "takeaway": {
    "title": "Architecture Boundary Invariant",
    "body": "Stateless compute nodes scale horizontally while shielding underlying database clusters behind fast cache layers."
  }
}
```

```mermaid
graph TD
    UserA((User A)) <--> WSS1[WS Server Shard 1]
    UserB((User B)) <--> WSS1
    UserC((User C)) <--> WSS2[WS Server Shard 2]
    
    WSS1 <--> LB[Internal Load Balancer]
    WSS2 <--> LB
    
    LB <--> OTS[OT Service: The Arbiter]
    OTS --> PDB[(Document Store: Postgres)]
    OTS --> RC[(Active Doc Cache: Redis)]
    
    OTS --> PubSub[Redis Pub/Sub]
    PubSub --> WSS1
    PubSub --> WSS2
```

**Observable outcome:** The critical insight is the separation of concerns : WebSocket Servers handle raw TCP connections and serialization, the OT Service is the single stateful arbiter that runs all transformations, and Redis Pub/Sub is the…

## Stage 6 — Deep Dive: How the OT Server Guarantees Document Convergence

- The "magic" of collaborative editing lies entirely inside the OT Service labeled "The Arbiter" in the architecture diagram.
- Understanding its internals reveals why a simple message broker is not enough—you need a stateful transformation engine with an ordered operation log.
- Internals: The Operation Log and Version Clock The OT Server maintains two critical data structures for each active document: an ordered operation log and a document snapshot .
- The operation log is an append-only ledger of every transformation ever applied to the document.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The operation log is an append-only ledger of every transformation ever applied to the document.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- Lesson 1 — Start with a single OT node and shard by document ID from day one.
- Adding document-level routing as an afterthought means rewriting the client session resume protocol.

## Alternatives considered

### OT vs. CRDT: A Decision Framework for Your Architecture

Use this guide to choose the right synchronization strategy before committing to either path.


## Failure and degraded modes

### Consistency vs. Latency: Trade-offs That Define Collaborative Systems

- **Detection:** Critical Failure Mode — The Thundering Herd on Reconnect: If a hot document has 1,000 simultaneous users and the OT service node crashes, all 1,000 WebSocket connections reconnect at the same instant.
- **User or operator impact:** Critical Failure Mode — The Thundering Herd on Reconnect: If a hot document has 1,000 simultaneous users and the OT service node crashes, all 1,000 WebSocket connections reconnect at the same instant.

seriesList.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
seriesList.description: Master the core of computer science. This series demystifies Data Structures and Algorithms, from Big O to graph theory. Learn to write efficient, scalable code and ace your technical interviews with confidence.

seriesList.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
